statement: The shared TACHOnet service shall provide participating card-issuing authorities with a reliable shared coordination service for checking card request status across borders without each organization having to chase others separately.
The system shall answer requests in a standardized way.
The system shall make request status visible through to completion.
The system shall control access properly.
The system shall flag overdue replies so cases do not stall.
The system shall make the core request-and-reply flow work consistently as the first priority.
The system shall track deadlines and late responses as the second priority.
The system shall provide access management as the third priority.
The system shall provide reporting and statistics as the final priority so organizations can monitor network performance.
The system shall allow European card-issuing authorities participating in the network to send requests.
The system shall have operational administrators for the shared service.
Management or oversight users may receive operational statistics and status reports.
The system shall let a user create and submit a request.
The system shall send the request to one or more selected member organizations.
The system shall keep the case open until all expected answers are back or the requester closes it.
The system shall store the outcome once finished so the full history can be reviewed later.
The service shall route requests based on the member or members selected by the requester.
The service shall use the network’s authorized participant list rather than inferring the target automatically.
Delivery to multiple members should usually be performed in parallel.
The service shall avoid sending requests to members that are not currently active or not authorized for the request type.
A request shall normally move from submitted to sent.
A request shall move to closed if it is cancelled or otherwise terminated.
Case closure shall be blocked while any required reply is still within its allowed response deadline.
The system shall provide a shared TACHOnet service for coordinating driver smart-card requests.
The system shall support replies.
The system shall support tracking.
The system shall enforce access control.
The system shall provide alerts for late responses.
The system shall provide reporting.
Participating members shall use the system day to day to send requests.
The current process for requesting, tracking, and coordinating driver smart-card status or delivery is handled through a mix of national systems, email, and manual follow-up between authorities.
The current process is not very uniform.
When checking a driver smart-card status, users need to determine whether the card has been issued, delivered, or is still pending.
To check driver smart-card status, someone contacts the other organization directly and tracks the answer separately.
Responses are often tracked in spreadsheets or local case systems.
The current process can be slow, inconsistent, and hard to use for obtaining a clear overall status unless people keep chasing responses manually.

The system shall reroute a request only when it can do so safely and with traceable responsibility.
The system shall return a request for clarification when the request is incomplete.
The system shall return a request for clarification when the authority cannot determine whether the request is in scope.
The system shall choose among rejection, rerouting, and clarification based on whether the issue is missing information, wrong destination, or a genuine legal or operational exclusion.
The system shall send an out-of-scope request back as incomplete or unprocessable with a clear standardized reason.
The system shall not guess when handling an out-of-scope request.
The system shall keep responsibility with the originating member to correct the request or resend it to the right place.
The system shall automatically forward a request only if it has enough routing evidence.
The system shall avoid making assumptions if it does not have enough routing evidence.
The rule for selecting the reason code or wording should be based on the best-known cause at the point the receiving authority evaluates the request.
If the request is missing mandatory data, the code should say incomplete information.
If the request is outside the authority’s remit but obviously sent to the wrong place, the code should say wrong destination.
If neither incomplete information nor wrong destination is clear, the system should use a generic processing boundary code.
The wording should stay standardized across all members so the originating side can act on it consistently.
The wording should be specific enough to tell the originating side whether to correct the content or resend it elsewhere.

The system shall fall back to the generic boundary code when using a more specific cause would require the receiving authority to reveal sensitive internal rules, legal interpretation, or operational details.
The system shall use the generic code when the evidence is weak or mixed and the authority cannot confidently classify the request as incomplete data or wrong destination.
The system shall use the longest mandatory retention period that applies to the authority for the record type in question.
The system shall delete records earlier if a national rule explicitly requires earlier deletion.
The system shall allow each authority to configure its own retention period within the shared framework.
The system shall account for differences in privacy and public-records obligations by country when determining retention periods.
The system shall retain at least request metadata and status history for the required period to support operational traceability and audit.
If there is an active legal hold, dispute, or audit requirement, the record should be kept until that hold is released, regardless of the normal retention end.
If there is no hold, the default action should be deletion or anonymization depending on what the national rule allows for the record type.
The choice between deletion and anonymization should be driven by the authority’s retention policy for that category of data.
Some records may need to be removed entirely, while others may only have personal data stripped.
If an acknowledgment is incomplete or ambiguous, the item shall remain pending and be marked as needing attention rather than being treated as a valid completion.
An unexpected format shall usually be handled the same way as an incomplete or ambiguous acknowledgment unless the system can safely map it to a known standardized response.
Retrying shall occur only when the problem appears technical, such as a transmission or parsing issue.
If the issue is a content problem, the request shall remain open until a valid acknowledgment is received.
If a message is clearly unusable, the system shall keep it out of the normal workflow so it does not accidentally advance or close anything.
Whether an unmatched acknowledgment stays pending shall depend on whether the original request is still otherwise awaiting a legitimate reply.
Limits on authority participation may apply based on each authority’s legal competence and the scope of the card or case type.
Some requests may be allowed only to the issuing authority.
Some requests may be allowed only to authorities that have a defined role for the relevant driver card action.
Participation is not always universal for every case type.
A delivery failure shall notify the originating authority.
If the delivery failure occurs on a reply path, the responding authority shall also be informed.
If repeated delivery failure attempts reach a defined number, the system shall escalate the failure to an operator alert.
If the delivery failure is clearly permanent, the system shall suppress repeated retries.
The notification rules depend on whether the failure occurred on an outgoing request or on a reply.
Retries shall be allowed only for technical transport failures.
Retries shall be allowed only on channels where the sender controls delivery.
Some message types may be too time-sensitive to retry many times.
Time-sensitive message types shall go to escalation sooner.
In some setups, the responding authority shall own the retry action rather than the originating authority.
The system shall define a target peak capacity and a safe degradation threshold so the service keeps running during spikes.
The system shall have a defined recovery expectation.
When the main service is unavailable, participating authorities shall keep their requests queued or deferred according to the agreed operating mode.
The system shall not fail silently when it is unavailable.
Queued requests shall remain stored until the service is restored.
The fallback mode shall apply only when the central TACHOnet service or its core messaging path is confirmed unavailable.
Any separately approved alternate path shall be explicitly configured and governed.
Planned maintenance windows should be scheduled outside normal business peaks where possible.
Urgent security or incident-driven maintenance may be given shorter notice.
The exact split between maintenance types requires agreement.
A maintenance-related outage shall be treated as confirmed once the planned maintenance starts at the published time.
A maintenance-related outage shall be treated as confirmed earlier if the service owner sends an explicit notice that the outage has begun or is unavoidable.
Participating authorities shall switch to the hold-or-contingency process immediately when the outage is confirmed, rather than waiting for a failed request.
The contingency process shall not be triggered when the maintenance information is only a warning or a possible delay.
A partial outage should trigger the hold-or-contingency process earlier if it affects message flow or response handling in a way that makes the service unreliable.
For a phased shutdown, the hold-or-contingency process should start when the affected function that participants depend on is actually taken out of service.
For a phased shutdown, the hold-or-contingency process should not start when preparatory work starts.
If a maintenance notice is withdrawn, the contingency should not start at all.
If a maintenance notice was announced in error and already triggered the contingency, the contingency should be ended immediately.
The recovery target should be relatively tight because participants depend on the service for operational coordination.
A complete outage should have the fastest restoration target.
A partial interruption may have a slightly longer restoration target if the core messaging and audit trail remain intact.
During planned maintenance, the system should return within the published maintenance window rather than follow a separate recovery target.

The operational rule for delayed, failed, or duplicated exchanges shall be based on the request state and the receipt of a valid acknowledgment, not solely on whether the participant observes a network timeout.
If a message was sent but no confirmation is received within the agreed timeout, the participant may retry once or follow the defined retry policy.
If the original request is later confirmed as accepted, duplicate exchanges shall be suppressed.
If the exchange is explicitly rejected or remains unresolved after the allowed retry window, it shall be treated as failed and escalated to operations for follow-up.
Requests rejected for business reasons must go straight to review or escalation rather than being retried automatically.
Requests that fail validation must go straight to review or escalation rather than being retried automatically.
Unauthorized requests must go straight to review or escalation rather than being retried automatically.
Malformed requests must go straight to review or escalation rather than being retried automatically.
Requests that are wrong or not permitted must not be retried automatically.
Status-check requests that are blocking an operational decision shall have a tighter deadline than routine informational queries.
Messages tied to an active card issuance case shall escalate sooner if they are nearing the timeout because they directly affect next steps.
Messages tied to a suspected duplicate shall escalate sooner if they are nearing the timeout because they directly affect next steps.
Urgent status confirmation messages shall escalate sooner if they are nearing the timeout because they directly affect next steps.
Urgent operational messages shall move to escalation as soon as the delay starts to risk the business process.
The service shall handle the normal daily operating peak without noticeable delay.
The service shall begin graceful degradation only after the normal daily operating peak is exceeded, rather than failing outright.
The service shall defer lower-priority work such as statistics, reporting, and non-urgent follow-ups first during overload conditions.
The service shall keep live request coordination available as long as possible during overload conditions.
A member organization shall not go fully live until its access rights are approved.
A member organization shall not go fully live until its technical connection has passed the required security checks.
A limited pilot or sandbox-style exchange may start earlier only if it is explicitly authorized.
A limited pilot or sandbox-style exchange may start earlier only if it is restricted to a controlled scope.
If any checks are still pending, a member organization shall not participate in the production coordination flow.
If something is still pending, the organization may remain in a controlled test or pilot mode.
A formally approved emergency arrangement from the program owners may be permitted as the only exception to the mandatory test-approval gate.
A member organization may receive live exchange access before interoperability and security checks are fully complete only under a formally approved temporary access arrangement.
Temporary live exchange access shall be very limited and time-bound.
Temporary live exchange access shall be used only for exceptional operational need.
Temporary live exchange access shall require explicit authorization from the program owners and clear tracking of permitted actions.
If those conditions are not met, a member organization shall wait until interoperability and security checks are fully complete before receiving live exchange access.
